c.tagline: Gateway to the sunken WWII fleets of Truk Lagoon.

taxi.fareNote: Shared taxis (white vehicles marked 'TAXI') charge a flat fare of roughly $1-3 per person around Weno regardless of exact distance; agree on the price before boarding, and service becomes scarce after about 5:30pm.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: Home to Chuuk International Airport and several of Weno's newest hotels, favored by divers with tight arrival/departure schedules and business travelers.
Weno's administrative and commercial core, with government offices, the main town dock, banks and shops within walking distance; convenient for first-timers.
A quieter residential stretch of coastline on Weno's east side, suited to travelers who want a beachfront feel away from the airport bustle.

The village at the southern tip of Weno, well away from the airport and the town strip, and the home of Blue Lagoon Resort with its own dive shop and restaurant. Quiet and rustic, and the usual base for divers working the Truk Lagoon wrecks.

water.note: Water access and treatment are unreliable in Chuuk; stick to bottled or boiled water.

transit.pay: There is no formal fare card or ticketing system; passengers simply flag down a shared taxi (white vehicles with a 'TAXI' sign) and pay the driver a flat cash fare, typically around $1-3 per person depending on distance. Inter-island boats and speedboats to other lagoon islands are arranged and paid for directly with operators, usually in cash.
transit.hours: No fixed schedule; shared taxis run informally through the day and are hard to find after about 5:30pm. Inter-island boat departures depend on tides, weather, and demand rather than a timetable.
transit.note: Weno has no public bus or rail system; most visitors rely on hotel shuttles, rental cars, or shared taxis, with speedboats used for hopping between lagoon islands.

bus: No fixed-route buses; informal shared taxis function as the de facto public transit
ferry: Field trip ships to Chuuk's outer islands

tip.r: Tipping isn't traditional in Chuukese culture, but is increasingly appreciated at hotels, dive operations, and restaurants that cater to foreign visitors; rounding up or a small cash tip for good service is welcomed, not required.

food.name: Reef fish and tuna sashimi
food.desc: Chuuk lives off the lagoon: parrotfish, snapper and emperor grilled or fried whole, and yellowfin cut for sashimi within hours of landing.

places.name: Truk Stop Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Weno's best-known kitchen, serving freshly caught seafood plus Micronesian and Asian plates.

places.name: Blue Lagoon Resort restaurant
places.note: Waterfront dining room at the dive resort with lagoon views and local seafood.

places.name: Weno public market
places.note: Fishermen sell the morning catch on strings; cheapest fish on the island.

food.name: Breadfruit (mai)
food.desc: The island's bread: breadfruit roasted in the fire, boiled, fried into chips, or pounded with coconut cream; also fermented into sour kon for storage.

places.name: Weno public market
places.note: Whole breadfruit and prepared portions sold in season; ask sellers how they cook theirs.

places.name: Truk Stop Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Local sides including breadfruit and taro appear alongside the international menu.

places.name: Blue Lagoon Resort restaurant
places.note: Serves traditional starches with fish for guests wanting a Chuukese plate.

food.name: Taro with coconut cream
food.desc: Swamp taro and true taro grown in wet pits, boiled and served in slabs or mashed with thick coconut cream; the ceremonial food of Chuuk.

places.name: Weno public market
places.note: Taro corms and prepared taro sold daily; a staple of every household.

places.name: Blue Lagoon Resort restaurant
places.note: Reliable spot to eat taro and coconut cream as part of a full meal.

places.name: Roadside kitchens, Mwan and Iras
places.note: Small takeaway counters plate taro and fish for a few dollars at lunchtime.

food.name: Coconut crab and mangrove crab
food.desc: Prized island catch: coconut crab, sweet and rich from a diet of coconut, and mangrove crab from the shorelines, usually boiled or grilled simply.

places.name: Truk Stop Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Crab appears when hunters bring it in; ask the kitchen rather than expecting it daily.

places.name: Weno public market
places.note: Crabs sold live and tied; supply is seasonal and sells out fast.

places.name: Blue Lagoon Resort restaurant
places.note: Will prepare crab for guests when it is available; worth requesting ahead.

food.name: Banana and breadfruit pudding
food.desc: Ripe banana, breadfruit or taro pounded and baked with coconut cream into dense sweet puddings, wrapped in leaves for feasts and church gatherings.

places.name: Weno public market
places.note: Home cooks sell leaf-wrapped puddings in the mornings; usually gone by midday.

places.name: Church and community feasts
places.note: Sunday gatherings are the real setting for traditional puddings; visitors are welcomed.

places.name: Truk Stop Hotel Restaurant
places.note: Occasional local desserts alongside imported sweets and pizza.

food.name: Fresh drinking coconut
food.desc: Green coconuts opened with a machete for the cool water inside, then split so you can scoop the soft flesh; sold everywhere along the Weno road.

places.name: Weno public market
places.note: Drinking nuts sold cheaply and opened for you on the spot.

places.name: Roadside stands, Mwan and Iras
places.note: Stands along the shore road sell coconuts and cold soft drinks all day.

places.name: Blue Lagoon Resort
places.note: Serves chilled coconuts by the water; easy after a morning wreck dive.

food.name: Coconut toddy
food.desc: Sap tapped at dawn from the coconut flower, drunk sweet the same morning or left to sour into a mild palm wine; Chuuk restricts alcohol sales tightly.

places.name: Village tappers, Sapuk and Nepukos
places.note: Toddy is a village tradition, not a shop product; go with a local contact.

places.name: Hard Wreck Cafe and Patio Bar
places.note: One of the few licensed bars on Weno; alcohol is otherwise heavily restricted.

places.name: Blue Lagoon Resort bar
places.note: Resort bar serving guests; respect local rules on drinking outside licensed premises.

landmarks: Fujikawa Maru

A 132-metre Japanese aircraft transport sunk during Operation Hailstone in February 1944, its holds still packed with disassembled Mitsubishi Zero fighters, widely rated one of the world's best wreck dives.
San Francisco Maru
A Japanese transport sunk on 18 February 1944, sitting upright at around 60 metres with three Type 95 light tanks still lashed to its deck and holds of mines and munitions below.
Shinkoku Maru

A 152-metre former Imperial Navy oil tanker that refuelled the Pearl Harbor strike force before sinking in Chuuk Lagoon, its bridge, engine room and sick bay still largely intact and heavily corallised.
Nefo Cave
A hand-dug Japanese wartime tunnel on Weno, roughly 24 metres deep, still holding an intact coastal-defence gun once trained on the lagoon's north pass against an invasion that never came.
Mount Tonaachaw

The hill above Chuuk International Airport, listed on the US National Register for both its Japanese gun emplacements and bunkers and prehistoric Chuukese fortifications and middens some 4,000 years old.
Tonotan Guns and Caves
A National Register-listed wartime site on the flank of Mount Teroken, with an excavated emplacement for a British-made naval gun and a network of caves the Japanese used for shelter.
Wiichen Men's Meetinghouse
A site at Peniesene with a pre-contact petroglyph panel and swimming basin, held in Chuukese oral tradition to be where the six brothers who became the islands' first chieftains met.
Xavier High School
A Jesuit school opened in 1952 on a hill the Japanese military built up as a wartime communications centre, listed on the National Register and still an active campus.
Kimiuo Aisek Memorial Museum
Chuuk's first museum, opened in 2014 beside the Blue Lagoon dive shop, showing a ship's bell, shell casings, gas masks and other artefacts recovered by divers from the lagoon's wrecks.
Eten Island
A small island south of Dublon that Japanese forces bulldozed flat to build an airstrip, now scattered with ruined military buildings and wrecked aircraft, with a short climb up 61-metre Mount Uinku.

train.note: There are no railways in the Federated States of Micronesia. Weno on Chuuk is reached by air into Chuuk International Airport, served by the United Island Hopper route between Honolulu and Guam. There is no rail anywhere in the region.

bus.note: No international coaches and no public bus service. Taxis on Weno are shared and very cheap, flagged down along the main road. Most visitors are divers and use resort transfers. There is no terminal.

intl.to: Chuuk lagoon outer islands - Tonoas, Fefan & Uman (Micronesia) - small boats
intl.op: local boat operators — arranged at the Weno dock

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry - all arrivals are by air. Small motorboats cross Chuuk lagoon to the outer islands on an informal basis, arranged at the dock or through a hotel, and government field-trip ships serve the distant atolls irregularly. Wreck-diving boats operate as charters over the sunken Japanese fleet.
